question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in our body?

options.A: Defending the body against foreign pathogens
options.B: Regulating body functions through hormone secretion
options.C: Filtering waste products directly from the bloodstream
options.D: Providing structural support for internal organs

explanation: Think of the endocrine system as your body's chemical messaging network! It uses glands to release hormones straight into the blood, controlling everything from growth to metabolism. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses do a full head-to-toe check for patients with hormone problems?

options.A: Endocrine glands are located exclusively in the head and neck regions
options.B: Hormone imbalances cause widespread physical changes across multiple body systems
options.C: Systemic assessments eliminate the need to check vital signs
options.D: Routine blood tests are unreliable for diagnosing hormonal conditions

explanation: Because hormones travel all over the body, when something is off, it affects more than just one spot. A head-to-toe check helps us catch all those clues! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h1)

question: If a patient's hands have a fine, gentle tremble during a quick physical check, what might this point to?
explanation: When the thyroid is in overdrive (hyperthyroidism), it speeds up your metabolism and makes the nervous system super jittery, which often shows up as shaky hands. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h2)

question: You walk into a warm ward and notice a patient is shivering and moving very slowly. Which condition should pop into your head?
explanation: When the thyroid is underactive, internal heat production drops. That's why these patients often feel freezing cold and sluggish, even when everyone else is comfortable. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h2)

question: What kind of skin do you usually see in someone with untreated hypothyroidism?
explanation: A slow metabolism means the sweat and oil glands aren't working at full speed, leaving the skin feeling dry, rough, and chilly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why does Addison's disease make a patient's skin turn a darker, bronze color?

options.A: Elevated levels of hormones that stimulate melanin production
options.B: Chronic dehydration leading to skin darkening
options.C: Increased exposure to sunlight caused by fatigue
options.D: Poor circulation trapping pigment in superficial capillaries

explanation: In Addison's, the brain pumps out extra signals to try and stimulate the adrenals; these hormones accidentally stimulate skin pigment (melanin) too, causing a dark tan look. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the clinical name for the bulging, wide-eyed look seen in Graves' disease?
explanation: Exophthalmos happens when the immune system causes inflammation and fluid buildup right behind the eyeballs, pushing them forward. Great word to add to your nursing vocabulary! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why would a nurse place the bell of a stethoscope over an enlarged thyroid gland?

options.A: To listen for a bruit caused by increased blood flow
options.B: To check for crackles moving up from the trachea
options.C: To measure the exact width of the thyroid lobes
options.D: To assess for abnormal whistling breath sounds

explanation: An overactive thyroid sucks up a massive amount of blood. That rushing blood creates an audible whooshing sound called a bruit that you can actually hear through your stethoscope! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which vital sign signs are classic for someone with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism?

options.D: Normal heart rate with low temperature

explanation: Everything is running in fast-forward with hyperthyroidism! The heart pumps faster (tachycardia) and stronger, giving you that bounding pulse. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h5)

question: If you check the blood pressure of a patient with Addison's disease, what are you most likely to find?
explanation: Without enough aldosterone, the body loses too much salt and water. Less fluid in the pipes means low blood pressure (hypotension). Makes complete sense when you trace the plumbing! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h5)

question: What do purple stretch marks (striae) on a patient's belly tell you during an endocrine assessment?

options.B: They show sudden weight loss from diabetes
options.C: They point toward chronic low blood pressure
options.D: They signal an acute thyroid infection

explanation: Too much cortisol weakens the protein fibers in the skin, making it fragile and resulting in those distinctive purple stretch marks, often seen in conditions like Cushing's. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h6)

question: How do hormone imbalances commonly affect a patient's muscles when you examine them?

options.A: Triggering severe joint infections throughout the body
options.B: Eliminating all deep tendon reflexes completely
options.C: Causing proximal muscle weakness that makes standing difficult
options.D: Causing rapid bone lengthening in older adults

explanation: Endocrine issues often target the big muscles closest to the center of the body (like thighs and shoulders), making tasks like standing up from a chair surprisingly tough. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which quick bedside test checks for low calcium by tapping gently on the facial nerve?
explanation: That's Chvostek's sign! Tap right on the cheek/facial nerve; if calcium is too low, the facial muscles will twitch uncontrollably. A classic physical assessment trick! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h7)

question: When testing deep tendon reflexes in a patient with hyperthyroidism, what do you expect to see?
explanation: Because excess thyroid hormone supercharges the nervous system, the reflexes will be brisk and hyperactive—jumpy reflexes match a jumpy metabolism! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is it important to match your physical assessment clues with lab hormone test results?

options.A: To replace the need for physician physical examinations
options.B: To calculate the exact date the disease started
options.C: To confirm diagnoses and evaluate treatment effectiveness
options.D: To eliminate the need for ongoing vital sign monitoring

explanation: Lab numbers tell one part of the story, and what you see with your own eyes tells the rest. Putting them together helps you see if the treatment plan is actually working. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is the best way to document your physical findings for an endocrine patient?

options.A: Document only the lab values and skip physical descriptions
options.B: Use general terms to save space in the medical record
options.C: Write personal opinions about the client's emotional state
options.D: Record objective and precise descriptions of physical signs

explanation: Clear, factual, and exact descriptions ensure that the whole healthcare team can track how the patient is doing over time without any guesswork. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h8)
